newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovans reject post-independence leader in vote.
newsitem.headline: Moldovans reject post-independence leader in vote.

text.p: Ex-communist social democrat Petru Lucinschi claimed victory on Monday in Moldova's first presidential election run-off over President Mircea Snegur, who led the former Soviet republic to independence 1991.
"Mircea Snegur is coming to Lucinschi's office this morning to congratulate him on his victory," a spokesman for the challenger, who is chairman of parliament, told Reuters.
Official data showed Lucinschi on 54.2 percent, a lead of more than eight points over Snegur, who had scored 45.8 percent with 82 percent of the vote counted. Turnout was 73 percent.
"The situation cannot now change greatly," state television said. Only votes from the capital Chisinau had yet to be added.

State radio said Lucinschi, who campaigned hard against Snegur's economic record and hopes for closer ties to ethnic kin in Romania, had also won comfortably in the city. Much of Moldova's one-third Russian-speaking minority live there.
The 56-year-old speaker, once a top Soviet communist official, had said Snegur might try to rig the vote or hold on to power, helped by loyal sections of the security forces.
But Chisinau was calm on Monday and state radio said Snegur would leave soon for Lisbon to attend the summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Electoral officials noted no major violations of voting rules. OSCE observers also had no reports of serious trouble.
The official handover of power is not due until January.

Lucinschi has reminded Moldovans that, even without the Soviet Union, they still depend on Moscow for vital energy supplies and much else. He also wants good relations with the West and portrays himself a European-style social democrat.

Backed by much of the media, the speaker played on accusations that Snegur's pro-Romanian drive had provoked the breakaway of the 700,000-strong Russian-speaking Dnestr region in 1990 and fighting there in 1992, when hundreds were killed.
Moldovans hurrying to work on a wet Monday morning in the city centre took the news of change with a note of resignation.
"I voted for Snegur," said Svetlana, a 27-year-old philologist. "But really, I don't think it makes a difference."
Valentina, who lives on a 90 lei ($18) monthly pension, had voted for Lucinschi. "Now I hope he raises my pension and makes sure I get it every month, that's the main thing," she said.
"The first thing he has to do is stabilise the economic situation. Life has been so hard for us," said 36-year-old Lena, a mathematician, who also voted for Lucinschi.
Valere, a 40-year-old teacher, said: "What we need is someone really fresh, with new ideas to solve our problems."
"Lucinschi isn't really new," he added. "But perhaps he'll bring some new people into the government, a new generation."

Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who backed Lucinschi after being knocked out of the presidential race in the first round on November 17, said before the vote that the government would resign after the election "to preserve civil peace".

Sangheli had been at odds with Snegur, who like Lucinschi is 56 and a former communist official. That had left the administration partly paralysed in addressing Moldova's grave economic crisis, which has seen incomes plummet since 1991.
The president, portraying himself as a centre-right reformer thwarted by a corrupt and unreconstructed leftist administration had sought greater constitutional powers.
Lucinschi, a bespectacled intellectual whose style contrasts sharply with the bluff and bear-like Snegur, had accused the president of wanting to install a dictatorship.
Authorities in Dnestr, where Russian troops keep the peace, boycotted the poll but a few thousand local people voted elsewhere in Moldova, foreign observers said.
